220:\caption{\textbf{Problem overview.} \textbf{(a)}~Today's TSFM benchmarks use a single static head over hidden states. \textbf{(b)}~The natural mixture-of-experts extension catastrophically fails on instance-normalized TSFMs: entropy collapses ($0.000{\pm}0.000$) and the remaining experts receive no gradient. Same backbone, different heads.}
221:\label{fig:problem_overview}
360:\caption{\textbf{RR-MoA architecture.} \textit{Path~A} (blue): frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf{H}$ for all experts. \textit{Path~B} (orange): Conv1d gate (1{,}100 params) reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects Top-2 experts; inactive experts (gray) receive no gradient. Standard hidden-state MoE collapses (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}); RR-MoA wins \textbf{54/54} (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}).}
361:\label{fig:framework}
401:\caption{\textbf{Freeze-level ablation} (test MSE, mean$\pm$std, 3 seeds, H=96). RR-MoA (sparse Top-2 routing over 5 experts) vs.\ the best single-head adapter from $\{$linear, attention, conv$\}$ trained with the same protocol. ``MSE $\Delta\%$ vs.\ single-head'' is the relative MSE change of RR-MoA over the single-head baseline; negative $=$ lower MSE $=$ better. RR-MoA wins \textbf{54/54} across 6 datasets (extended grid in Appendix~\ref{app:extended_rrmoa}); the gain is largest when frozen (``Frozen Paradox'').}
437:\caption{\textbf{AdaMix routing collapse} (entropy max ${\approx}1.609$). Under unfreezing, entropy ${\to}0.000$. \colorbox{green!8}{Green}: disabling RevIN inside MOMENT recovers entropy ($0.66$--$1.32$), proving RevIN is the causal mechanism. Extended grid in Appendix~\ref{app:extended_rrmoa}.}
471:\caption{\textbf{Per-step routing / gradient trajectory} (AdaMix, ETTh1). (a)~Unfrozen+RevIN (red) collapses within ${\sim}50$ steps; strictly frozen control (blue) stays stable, isolating gradient co-adaptation from optimizer or data effects. (b)~Dominant expert's gradient grows while others starve (co-adaptation loop, \S\ref{sec:rrmoa}). Removing RevIN (separate experiment, Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}) shows the trajectory inverts.}
472:\label{fig:trajectory}
480:\caption{\textbf{Causal contrast: MOMENT vs Timer-XL} (ETTh1, last-4 unfreezing). Solid lines: unfrozen runs. MOMENT entropy collapses $0.51{\to}0.000$ in ${\sim}40$ steps (red); Timer-XL stays at ${\approx}1.60$ for all $400$ steps (orange). Dashed lines: frozen-backbone controls for both models, neither collapses. Dotted: $\log K{=}1.609$ ceiling. Same code, same data, only normalization differs. Pattern generalizes across all 3 tested datasets.}
481:\label{fig:causal_contrast}
494:\caption{\textbf{Eight converging causal controls.} Each tests a different alternative hypothesis for routing collapse; all converge on normalization as the cause.}
518:\caption{\textbf{Baseline comparison} (MOMENT-small, Top-2, 5 seeds, H=96). Above double rule: frozen; full FT unfreezes all 8 blocks. Wilcoxon, Bonferroni-corrected. Grey rows: from-scratch calibration anchors.}
641:\caption{\textbf{Left: Frozen Paradox}, frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by $12$--$79\%$. \textbf{Right: Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases.}
642:\label{fig:frozen_paradox}
643:\label{fig:signal_ratio}
1023:\caption{RR-MoA: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters with Top-$k$ sparse routing}
1044:\caption{\textbf{Multi-horizon RR-MoA vs.\ DLinear} (MOMENT-small, strictly frozen, Top-2, 5 seeds, test MSE mean$\pm$std). RR-MoA wins all 24 configurations vs.\ best fixed baseline across horizons $96$--$720$. DLinear column provides supervised calibration: the gap narrows from $+63\%$ to $+48\%$ on ETTh1 and from $+33\%$ to $+15\%$ on Weather as $H$ grows, consistent with the frozen backbone's horizon-invariant representation becoming relatively more informative at longer horizons.}
1149:\caption{\textbf{Normalization dose-response} (frozen, 5 seeds $\times$ 6 datasets; std smaller than markers). MSE vs $\alpha$ ($0{=}$raw, $1{=}$RevIN). Phase transition at $\alpha{=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), mild for $\alpha{\leq}0.75$ ($+5.4\%$); routing entropy stays in $[1.43,1.57]$ across all $\alpha$ (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).}
1150:\label{fig:dose_response}
1195:\caption{Full LoRA sweep (strictly frozen backbone, 3 seeds, test MSE mean$\pm$std). Bold rows are the best-per-dataset configuration used in Table~\ref{tab:baselines}. No LoRA variant beats the RR-MoA (Top-2) result on any dataset.}
1255:\caption{\textbf{Normalization-induced routing collapse mechanism.} \textit{Left:} Raw input windows with distinct characteristics (amplitude, trend, volatility) are routed to different experts. \textit{Right:} After instance normalization strips $\mu$ and $\sigma$, all windows become indistinguishable, and the router collapses to a single expert (entropy $\to 0.000$).}
1256:\label{fig:collapse_mechanism}
1261:\caption{\textbf{Rawness vs.\ bypass} (frozen, Top-2, 3 seeds). RevIN router reads the same input after per-window normalization. Stripping statistics degrades MSE by 60--88\%.}
1391:\caption{\textbf{SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma_k$ reading $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, with no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf{H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph{raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle, not the specific router, drives the gains.}
1392:\label{fig:srmoa_arch}
1397:\caption{\textbf{Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA): routing input control} (dense, 5 seeds unless noted). Each expert has its own sigmoid gate, with no external router. \textbf{Top}: gating on raw input vs hidden states (frozen, MOMENT-small). \textbf{Second}: Timer-XL negative control with no RevIN, so raw$\approx$hidden. \textbf{Third}: freeze-level ablation confirms Frozen Paradox (frozen best 4/6). \textbf{Bottom}: cross-backbone generalization (H=96, frozen). 252 runs total.}
1465:\caption{\textbf{Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility (the very statistics RevIN strips), empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(iii). Note: conv1d (purple) is in the legend but rarely the top-1 expert on ETTh1, so it is not visually present.}
1466:\label{fig:routing_viz}
1490:\caption{\textbf{Statistics re-injection fails} (MOMENT-small, frozen, Top-2, 3 seeds). Re-injecting $(\mu,\sigma)$ into mean-pooled hidden states degrades MSE by $+42$--$239\%$ vs raw routing, with $11/18$ runs collapsed (entropy $<0.3$). Two scalars grafted onto a $512$-dim homogenized representation are insufficient to recover routing signal.}
1514:\caption{\textbf{Extended freeze-level ablation} (ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity; test MSE, mean$\pm$std, 3 seeds, H=96). Continues Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa} from the main text.}
1543:\caption{\textbf{Extended AdaMix routing collapse} (ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity). Continues Table~\ref{tab:adamix} from the main text.}
1577:\caption{\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep} (MOMENT-small $+$ RevIN, 720 runs). ``Collapsed'' = fraction of cells with entropy $<0.3$ (max $\log K{=}1.609$). No rescue mechanism recovers routing to within $2.7\times$ of RR-MoA.}
1611:\caption{\textbf{AdaMix-Raw: architecture-agnostic validation} (MOMENT-small, 3 seeds). Replacing AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router recovers routing entropy and MSE on all 12 cells, confirming the fix generalizes beyond RR-MoA.}
1639:\caption{\textbf{Routing collapse generalizes across normalizer types.} All three instance-level normalizers (RevIN, BatchNorm1d, GroupNorm) cause entropy collapse under unfreezing; removing normalization prevents collapse. Per-step trajectories logged over 400 optimizer steps on ETTh1, last-4 unfreezing, seed 42.}
1664:\caption{\textbf{Vision MoE routing collapse control} (CIFAR-10, $K{=}5$ diverse experts, mean$\pm$std over 3 seeds). \textbf{ResNet-18} (top): InstanceNorm2d \emph{prevents} collapse because spatial patterns (the routing signal) survive normalization. \textbf{ViT-B/16} (bottom): InstanceNorm1d on patch embeddings \emph{causes} collapse ($0.000\pm0.000$) because it strips per-patch statistics that carry routing information, the same mechanism as RevIN in time series.}
1693:\caption{\textbf{Top-$k$ sparse routing ablation on ETTh1 (last-2 freeze, 3 seeds).} Top-2 is the operating point used throughout the paper.}
1719:\caption{\textbf{Expert pool diversity ablation} (MOMENT-small frozen, Top-2, H=96, 3 seeds). Canonical diverse pool wins on ETTh1 and ETTm1; identical pools are competitive on Weather.}
1743:\caption{\textbf{Expert count scaling} (MOMENT-small frozen, Top-2, H=96, 3 seeds). Performance is stable for $K{\geq}2$; $K{=}1$ (no routing) is catastrophically worse.}
1767:\caption{\textbf{Imputation task} (20\% masked reconstruction, MOMENT-small frozen, test MSE mean$\pm$std over 5 seeds). RR-MoA wins \textbf{7/8 datasets} ($-21\%$ to $-79\%$); the sole loss is Solar where dense\_mlp dominates.}
1795:\caption{\textbf{Learned normalization coefficient} ($\alpha$, 5 seeds). All 30 runs converge to $\alpha < 0.5$, confirming gradient descent prefers raw input for routing.}
1821:\caption{\textbf{Exact MI loss measurement and bound tightness} (3 seeds). $H(E \mid S)$ is the exact routing information lost to normalization. Retention $= I(S;E)/H(E)$. LB = lower bound from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii). Gap $= I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ via within-expert CCA.}
1852:\caption{\textbf{Backbone features vs.\ raw input} (H=96, 80/20 train/test split). k-NN: k-nearest neighbor regression ($k{=}20$, distance-weighted) on mean-pooled backbone features vs.\ raw 512-dim input. Ridge: regularized linear regression (cross-validated $\alpha$). Backbone features are $16$--$33\%$ worse than raw input even with a universal approximator (k-NN), confirming genuine information destruction.}
1872:\caption{\textbf{Few-shot learning curve} (H=96, mean$\pm$std over seeds $\{42,43,44\}$). DLinear (49K params, trained from scratch) dominates frozen RR-MoA-full (426K params) at every training set size, confirming the gap reflects encoder information loss rather than data efficiency.}
1894:\caption{\textbf{Cross-backbone RR-MoA} (strictly frozen, Top-2 sparse, H=96, 5 seeds). Best fixed: strongest single-adapter baseline. RR-MoA wins all 15 configurations. MOMENT-large expanded to 6 datasets confirms generalization ($-32\%$ to $-75\%$).}
1915:\caption{\textbf{Extension to a native-MoE backbone: Moirai-MoE} (strictly frozen, Top-2 sparse, H=96, 5 seeds, 60 runs total). Moirai-MoE is a TSFM whose internal FFN layers are themselves sparsely-gated experts~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe}, with LayerNorm only (no RevIN). RR-MoA wins \textbf{all 6 datasets} by $-37\%$ to $-90\%$, confirming that adapter-level routing stacks on top of backbone-internal routing. AdaMix's hidden-state routing does \emph{not} collapse on Moirai-MoE: routing entropy is exactly $\log K = 1.6094$ to four decimal places across all 30 cells ($\sigma{=}0.0000$), indicating mathematically uniform routing, yet AdaMix still only matches the best fixed baseline MSE, demonstrating that raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse.}
1934:\caption{\textbf{Negative control: Timer-XL}~\citep{liu2025timerxl} (decoder-only, 84M params, LayerNorm only, no RevIN; H=96, 5 seeds). \textbf{Key causal result}: on MOMENT (RevIN), unfreezing drives entropy DOWN toward $0.000$ ($71\%$ collapsed). On Timer-XL, unfreezing drives entropy \textbf{UP} toward the maximum $1.609$ ($0/90$ collapsed). The trajectories are \emph{opposite}, isolating RevIN as the causal mechanism. AdaMix wins $5/6$ when frozen, confirming RR-MoA is unnecessary without instance normalization.}
1960:\caption{\textbf{Extension to Exchange and Solar datasets} (MOMENT-small, strictly frozen, Top-2 sparse, H=96, 5 seeds for RR-MoA/AdaMix, 3 seeds for DLinear/AdaMix-last4). Exchange ($R{=}2.17$, highest signal ratio) confirms the theory prediction: $-66.5\%$ improvement. Solar ($R{=}0.06$, lowest) is an outlier: RR-MoA still achieves $-32.9\%$ improvement, indicating the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale (consistent with the SSR ablation in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}). AdaMix collapses to $0.000$ entropy under last-4 unfreezing on both datasets.}
1996:\caption{\textbf{Inference latency and memory across all three architectural variants} (MOMENT-small, A10G GPU, batch size $128$, $200$ repeats with $20$-step CUDA-event warmup; synthetic random inputs at the standard LTSF batch shape, since latency for non-autoregressive deterministic forward passes is data-oblivious). All three architectural fixes (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) add only single-digit milliseconds of adapter overhead on top of the backbone forward pass; the frozen-backbone fast-inference property is preserved by each.}
2025:\caption{\textbf{Extended full fine-tuning} does not close the Frozen Paradox gap. Best of 5 training configurations (15ep Adam, 50ep Adam, 50ep cosine, 50ep cosine+layerwise, 50ep lr=1e-5). Frozen RR-MoA wins by $33$--$41\%$ even against the strongest optimization schedule.}
2067:\caption{\textbf{Closing the DLinear gap} (MOMENT-small, strictly frozen, Top-2, 3 seeds, H=96). Dual-stream experts that access both hidden states and raw input narrow the gap from $+33$--$75\%$ to $+9$--$11\%$ and \textbf{beat DLinear on Weather}. Learned $\alpha{\approx}0.49$ confirms the backbone contributes complementary information when combined with raw access.}
```

## Visual Error Report — `main.pdf`

**Methodology**: rendered all 44 pages at 200dpi → `/tmp/main_pdf_pages/`; one subagent per figure-bearing page (9 agents); 3 follow-up agents to verify HIGH-severity claims at 300dpi.

**Severity legend**: 🔴 critical · 🟡 medium · ⚪ cosmetic.  Severity downgraded after re-verification is shown as `[downgraded from X]`.

### Main paper (pp 1-13)

**Fig 1 — Problem overview** (TikZ `main.tex:79-238`)
- ⚪ Inactive expert boxes H1/H3/H4/H5 in panel (b) misaligned vertically; spacing inconsistent vs active H2.
- ⚪ Router→expert arrows all equal weight; no visual emphasis on the single "collapsed" path.
- ⚪ Input waveforms slightly overflow their bounding frames at amplitude peaks.
- ⚪ "(a)" / "(b)" panel labels much smaller and lighter than in-panel title strips.

**Fig 2 — RR-MoA architecture** (TikZ `main.tex:240-360`)
- ⚪ "PATH A: BACKBONE" / "PATH B: ROUTING" stream-header badges sit at the figure corners and read as squeezed against the bounding box.
- 🟡 Active vs inactive expert contrast is low — at column width it is hard to see which 2 of 5 experts are the orange Top-2.
- ⚪ "(no gradient)" italic subtitle inside the blue Frozen TSFM box is borderline-illegible.
- ⚪ "K=5 experts" vertical annotation crowds the Conv1d expert box.
- ⚪ "1,100 params" annotation tightly packed against gate edge.

**Fig 3 — AdaMix trajectory** (`figures/adamix_trajectory.pdf`, generator `scripts/plot_adamix_trajectory.py`)
- 🟡 Panel (a) legend overlaps the blue Frozen+RevIN trace at steps 0-100.
- 🟡 Panel (b) 5-expert legend sits inside the plot area, overlapping gradient-norm traces.
- 🟡 **Color-semantic break across panels**: red = "collapsed/bad" in (a), but in (b) red is just one expert. Same for blue. This breaks the paper-wide convention.
- ⚪ Aspect ratio short/wide squashes vertical dynamic range, especially the log y-axis in (b).

**Fig 4 — Causal contrast** (`figures/causal_contrast.pdf`, generator `scripts/plot_causal_contrast.py`)

26	def load_results():

32	    dose = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(list))  # dose[dataset][alpha] = [mse, ...]
33	    entropy = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(list))  # entropy[dataset][alpha] = [ent, ...]
34	
35	    for ds in DATASETS:
36	        for seed in SEEDS:
37	            # alpha=0.0: from the dose-response sweep (router-partial_alpha-0.00)
38	            raw_path = os.path.join(results_dir,
39	                "%s_H96_K5_dense_frozen_%d_router-partial_alpha-0.00.json" % (ds, seed))
40	            if os.path.exists(raw_path):
41	                with open(raw_path) as f:
42	                    data = json.load(f)
43	                dose[ds][0.0].append(data["rr_moa"]["mse"])
44	                entropy[ds][0.0].append(data["rr_moa"]["routing_entropy"])
45	
46	            # alpha > 0: partial suffix
47	            for alpha in ALPHAS[1:]:
48	                path = os.path.join(results_dir,
49	                    "%s_H96_K5_dense_frozen_%d_router-partial_alpha-%.2f.json" % (ds, seed, alpha))
50	                if os.path.exists(path):
51	                    with open(path) as f:
52	                        data = json.load(f)
53	                    dose[ds][alpha].append(data["rr_moa"]["mse"])
54	                    entropy[ds][alpha].append(data["rr_moa"]["routing_entropy"])
55	
56	    # Shuffle results

58	    for ds in DATASETS:

61	                "%s_H96_K5_dense_frozen_%d_router-shuffled.json" % (ds, seed))

67	                    "entropy": data["rr_moa"]["routing_entropy"],
68	                })

70	    return dose, entropy, shuffle

73	def check_monotonicity(values):

75	    for i in range(1, len(values)):
76	        if values[i] < values[i-1] - 1e-6:
77	            return False
78	    return True

60	            x_data[mask], y_data[mask],
61	            c=[colors[eid]], s=6, alpha=0.3,
62	            label=expert_names[eid], rasterized=True,
63	        )
64	    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
65	    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
66	    ax.tick_params(direction="in")
67	
68	# Single shared legend, outside the right panel
69	handles, labels = axes[1].get_legend_handles_labels()
70	fig.legend(
71	    handles, labels,
72	    loc="upper center", ncol=n_experts,
73	    fontsize=7, frameon=False,
74	    bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.02),
75	    markerscale=2.0,
76	)
77	
78	# ── Cluster annotation (if one expert dominates a region) ──────────────
79	# Check left panel: attention expert tends to cluster at high amplitude
80	counts = Counter(top1)
81	dominant_id = counts.most_common(1)[0][0]
82	dom_mask = top1 == dominant_id
83	dom_amp = amplitude[dom_mask]
84	dom_vol = volatility[dom_mask]
85	# Annotate centroid of the dominant cluster in left panel
86	cx, cy = np.median(dom_amp), np.median(dom_vol)
87	axes[0].annotate(
88	    f"{expert_names[dominant_id]} cluster",
89	    xy=(cx, cy), fontsize=6, fontstyle="italic",
90	    color=colors[dominant_id],
91	    ha="center", va="bottom",
92	    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.7),
93	)
94	
95	plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.93])
96	fig.savefig(OUT_PATH, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
97	plt.close(fig)
98	print(f"Saved: {OUT_PATH}")
99

1	"""T2.A visualization: plot per-step routing / gradient trajectories
2	produced by ``run_adamix.py --trajectory ...``.
3	
4	Reads two JSONL files (an "unfrozen" collapse case and a "frozen" control)
5	and produces a single two-panel figure:
6	
7	    Panel (a): routing entropy over optimizer steps, one line per setting.
8	    Panel (b): per-expert gradient L2 norm over steps, collapse case only
9	               (to show that one expert's gradient dominates and the others
10	               rapidly starve). A dashed line gives the sum of the other 4
11	               experts for reference.
12	
13	Usage::
14	
15	    python scripts/plot_adamix_trajectory.py \
16	        --collapse results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_last4_42.jsonl \
17	        --control  results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_frozen_42.jsonl \
18	        --out figures/adamix_trajectory.pdf
19	
20	The output PDF is intended to be dropped into ``main.tex`` as a standalone
21	figure between Tables 4 and 5, upgrading the gradient co-adaptation claim
22	from correlational (Table 4 entropies at epoch end) to mechanistic.
23	"""
24	
25	import argparse
26	import json
27	import math
28	import os
29	import sys
30	
31	import numpy as np
32	import matplotlib
33	matplotlib.use("Agg")
34	import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
35	
36	
37	def load_jsonl(path):
38	    records = []
39	    with open(path) as f:
40	        for line in f:
41	            line = line.strip()
42	            if not line:
43	                continue
44	            records.append(json.loads(line))
45	    return records
46	
47	
48	def plot_trajectory(collapse_path, control_path, out_path, K=5):
49	    collapse = load_jsonl(collapse_path)
50	    control = load_jsonl(control_path) if control_path else None
51	
52	    max_steps = max(len(collapse), len(control) if control else 0)
53	    log_max = math.log(K)
54	
55	    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.3), dpi=150)
56	
57	    # --- Panel (a): routing entropy over steps ---
58	    ax = axes[0]
59	    steps_c = [r["step"] for r in collapse]
60	    ent_c = [r["routing_entropy"] for r in collapse]
61	    ax.plot(steps_c, ent_c, color="tab:red", linewidth=2,
62	            label="AdaMix, last-4 unfrozen (ETTh1)")
63	    if control is not None:
64	        steps_f = [r["step"] for r in control]
65	        ent_f = [r["routing_entropy"] for r in control]
66	        ax.plot(steps_f, ent_f, color="tab:blue", linewidth=2,
67	                label="AdaMix, strictly frozen (ETTh1, control)")
68	    ax.axhline(log_max, color="gray", linestyle=":", linewidth=1,
69	               label=r"$\log K = \log 5$ (uniform max)")
70	    ax.set_xlabel("(a) Optimizer step")
71	    ax.set_ylabel("Router entropy (nats)")
72	    ax.set_ylim(-0.05, log_max + 0.1)
73	    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
74	    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=7, frameon=True)
75	
76	    # --- Panel (b): per-expert grad norm for the collapse case ---
77	    ax = axes[1]
78	    grad_matrix = np.array([r["expert_grad_norms"] for r in collapse])  # (T, K)
79	    colors = ["tab:red", "tab:orange", "tab:green", "tab:blue", "tab:purple"]
80	    labels = ["Mean", "Last", "Max", "Attn", "Conv1d"]
81	    # Order by peak gradient norm -> the dominant expert becomes the red line
82	    peak_idx = np.argsort(-grad_matrix.max(axis=0))
83	    for rank, k in enumerate(peak_idx):
84	        style = "-" if rank == 0 else "--"
85	        lw = 2.0 if rank == 0 else 1.0
86	        alpha = 1.0 if rank == 0 else 0.7
87	        ax.plot(steps_c, grad_matrix[:, k], color=colors[rank % len(colors)],
88	                linestyle=style, linewidth=lw, alpha=alpha,
89	                label=("%s (dominant)" % labels[k]) if rank == 0 else labels[k])
90	    ax.set_xlabel("(b) Optimizer step")
91	    ax.set_ylabel(r"$\|\nabla_{\phi_k}\mathcal{L}\|_2$ (log scale)")
92	    ax.set_yscale("log")
93	    ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
94	    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=7, frameon=True, ncol=2)
95	
96	    fig.tight_layout()
97	    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out_path) or ".", exist_ok=True)
98	    fig.savefig(out_path, bbox_inches="tight")
99	    pdf_path = out_path
100	    if not out_path.endswith(".pdf"):
101	        pdf_path = os.path.splitext(out_path)[0] + ".pdf"
102	        fig.savefig(pdf_path, bbox_inches="tight")
103	    print("Saved: %s" % out_path)
104	    return out_path
105	
106	
107	def main():
108	    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
109	    p.add_argument("--collapse", required=True,
110	                   help="JSONL trajectory for an unfrozen / collapse condition")
111	    p.add_argument("--control", default=None,
112	                   help="JSONL trajectory for the frozen / control condition")
113	    p.add_argument("--out", default="figures/adamix_trajectory.pdf")
114	    p.add_argument("--K", type=int, default=5)
115	    args = p.parse_args()
116	
117	    plot_trajectory(args.collapse, args.control, args.out, K=args.K)
118	
119	
120	if __name__ == "__main__":
121	    main()
122

1	"""Plot the causal contrast figure: MOMENT vs Timer-XL entropy trajectories.
2	
3	4 lines on one panel:
4	  - MOMENT frozen (blue, dashed) — control, entropy stays moderate
5	  - MOMENT last-4 (red, solid) — collapse, entropy → 0
6	  - Timer-XL frozen (green, dashed) — control, entropy stays at max
7	  - Timer-XL last-4 (orange, solid) — NO collapse, entropy stays at max
8	
9	Usage:
10	    python scripts/plot_causal_contrast.py --out figures/causal_contrast.pdf
11	"""
12	
13	import json, math, os, sys
14	import numpy as np
15	import matplotlib
16	matplotlib.use("Agg")
17	import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
18	
19	
20	def load_jsonl(path):
21	    records = []
22	    with open(path) as f:
23	        for line in f:
24	            line = line.strip()
25	            if line:
26	                records.append(json.loads(line))
27	    return records
28	
29	
30	def main():
31	    import argparse
32	    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
33	    p.add_argument("--moment-frozen", default="results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_frozen_42.jsonl")
34	    p.add_argument("--moment-last4", default="results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_last4_42.jsonl")
35	    p.add_argument("--timer-frozen", default="results/adamix_timer/trajectory_ETTh1_frozen_42_timer.jsonl")
36	    p.add_argument("--timer-last4", default="results/adamix_timer/trajectory_ETTh1_last4_42_timer.jsonl")
37	    p.add_argument("--out", default="figures/causal_contrast.pdf")
38	    p.add_argument("--K", type=int, default=5)
39	    args = p.parse_args()
40	
41	    log_max = math.log(args.K)
42	
43	    trajectories = {
44	        "MOMENT frozen": (args.moment_frozen, "tab:blue", "--", 1.5),
45	        "MOMENT last-4 (RevIN)": (args.moment_last4, "tab:red", "-", 2.5),
46	        "Timer-XL frozen": (args.timer_frozen, "tab:cyan", "--", 1.5),
47	        "Timer-XL last-4 (no RevIN)": (args.timer_last4, "tab:orange", "-", 2.5),
48	    }
49	
50	    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(5.5, 3.5), dpi=150)
51	
52	    for label, (path, color, ls, lw) in trajectories.items():
53	        data = load_jsonl(path)
54	        steps = [r["step"] for r in data]
55	        ent = [r["routing_entropy"] for r in data]
56	        ax.plot(steps, ent, color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=lw, label=label)
57	
58	    ax.axhline(log_max, color="gray", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.8,
59	               label=r"$\log K$ (max entropy)")
60	    ax.set_xlabel("Optimizer step", fontsize=11)

1399	\caption{\textbf{SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma_k$ reading $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, with no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf{H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph{raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle, not the specific router, drives the gains.}
1400	\label{fig:srmoa_arch}
1401	\end{figure}

366	\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
367	\label{sec:rrmoa}
368	
369	An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. The goal of per-window routing is to select, for each input window, the subset of expert adapters best suited to that window's characteristics, so that a quiet baseline and a volatile spike are handled by different adapter topologies rather than forced through the same head. As shown in the introduction, this fails when the router reads normalized hidden states, because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:

225	\section{Related Work}
226	
227	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; benchmarking work includes TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval}. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies} while keeping a single adapter architecture. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window.
228	
229	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been used \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale capacity, with experts placed inside the backbone architecture: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes are complementary rather than competing: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
230	
231	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse is a well-known failure mode addressed by load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}; AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} carries discriminative information. Sweeping the five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN, none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Concurrent work in NLP/vision toward router-free MoEs (AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe}, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe}, Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree}) supports this view: in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}), self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses. \citet{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry; we extend this upstream by identifying what shapes that geometry on TSFMs.
232	
233	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental, and \citet{zou2025ibnorm} argue that variance-centric normalization (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) is suboptimal for representation learning because two representations with identical mean and variance can encode different amounts of task-relevant information. We identify a specific, mechanistic consequence of this principle that has not been characterized in the MoE literature: when the stripped statistics carry the \emph{routing} signal in a downstream MoE adapter, instance normalization causes catastrophic routing collapse, a failure mode distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE rescue literature.}
234	
235	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
236

2261	\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit{Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf{H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit{Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw} + \sigma(\mathrm{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})) \cdot \mathrm{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma$ gates (orange) on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf{6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf{107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times$ 6 datasets $\times$ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}
2262	\label{fig:residual_ia_arch}
2263	\end{figure}
2264	
2265	The dual-stream and multi-resolution variants narrow the average DLinear gap from $+57\%$ to $+5$--$8\%$ (Tables~\ref{tab:gap_closing}, \ref{tab:gap_closing_ext}) but win on only 1/6 datasets (Weather). A systematic $546$-run hyperparameter sweep uncovered a \emph{second} hidden pathology and the architectural fix that closes the remaining gap to \textbf{4/6 match-or-beat}.
2266	
2267	\textbf{Diagnostic: gates fail to learn.} We instrumented the per-sample gate mechanism to log its mean activation per expert per dataset. Across every configuration tested (\{rh128, rh192, rh256, rh320, rh384, rh512\} $\times$ \{d1, d2, d3 raw-branch depth\} $\times$ \{lr, wd, cosine, warmup\} hyperparameter combinations), the learned gates consistently plateau at $\sigma(0.0){\approx}0.5$:
2268	
2269	\begin{center}
2270	\small
2271	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccc@{}}
2272	\toprule
2273	Config & ETTh1 & ETTh2 & ETTm1 & ETTm2 & Weather & Elec. \\
2274	\midrule
2275	Dual-stream ($\alpha_k$)             & $0.49$ & $0.50$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ \\
2276	Residual-IA (gate-init $b{=}0$)      & $0.47$ & $0.50$ & $0.48$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.47$ \\
2277	Residual-IA + cos+wd ($b{=}0$)       & $0.50$ & $0.51$ & $0.49$ & $0.52$ & $0.50$ & $0.49$ \\
2278	\bottomrule
2279	\end{tabular}
2280	\end{center}
2281	
2282	With 15 epochs of training, the gate mechanism extracts no gradient signal about \emph{which branch should dominate} because both branches receive co-equal credit for reducing loss from the start. This is isomorphic to the dual-stream $\alpha_k \approx 0.49$ observation, indicating it is not a quirk of a single architecture but a general failure mode of symmetrically-initialized mixture mechanisms on this task.
2283	
2284	\textbf{Three surgical fixes.}

SR-MoA shares only the raw-input principle with RR-MoA (Figure 2): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. > DEVELOPER

is it true that Rescue Mechanimsm are mainly used for other modality different from time series

> AGENT

Yes — true. All five rescue families in the paper's sweep come from NLP/vision MoE literature:

- **Load balancing** — Switch Transformer (Fedus 2022, T5 NLP)
- **Z-loss** — ST-MoE (Zoph 2022, NLP)
- **ReLU routing** — ReMoE (Zhang 2025, NLP)
- **Expert-Choice routing** — Zhou 2022 (NLP)
- **Entropy regularization** — generic, originally NLP/vision MoE

None were designed or evaluated on time-series foundation models. AdaMix (Wang 2022), the only adapter-level MoE the paper benchmarks against, is also NLP. The paper's contribution is precisely that this entire toolkit assumes the router's *input* carries discriminative signal — an assumption that holds in NLP token streams but breaks under RevIN on TSFMs because instance normalization strips the per-window statistics the router would need.

> DEVELOPER

so is it fair that we used it as control ?

> AGENT

Yes, fair — but only with the framing the paper already uses. The argument has to be:

> Rescue mechanisms target **optimization-induced collapse** (dead experts from gradient pathology, load imbalance, gating starvation). We test whether they also fix **representation-induced collapse** (router input lacks discriminative signal because RevIN stripped it). They don't — because the failure is upstream of optimization. The negative result is evidence that the two collapse modes are categorically distinct, not evidence that NLP techniques are weak.

So the rescue sweep is a fair **negative control for the hypothesis "this collapse is just standard MoE optimization pathology"**. Without that hypothesis to refute, the sweep would indeed look like an unfair domain-transfer test.

Where this could go wrong with reviewers:
1. If the paper says "rescue mechanisms fail on TSFMs" without naming the categorical distinction → reviewer reads it as "you're benchmarking NLP tools out of domain"
2. If the rescue sweep's framing in the prose doesn't match its role in the table caption.

Quick check the paper currently has the right framing — your related-work section already says *"All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's input carries discriminative information"* (line 231 area), and the rescue table is positioned as a falsification of the optimization-pathology alternative explanation. That's the right framing. Just make sure the body text near `tab:rescue` uses the words **"optimization-induced vs representation-induced"** explicitly, not just "rescue fails."

Want me to check whether the body text near `tab:rescue` makes the categorical distinction crisp enough, and tighten it if not?

487	In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $27\%$ to $77\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters, exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
488	
489	\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep five standard MoE rescue families (Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}) across eleven configurations on 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, none of the standard rescue mechanisms we tested can compensate.
490	
491	\textbf{Three architectural instantiations of one principle.} The diagnosis says: restore raw-input access wherever normalization destroyed it. The paper proposes three variants, all confirming the same diagnosis from different angles. \emph{(i)}~\textbf{RR-MoA} (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:framework}, headline contribution): external Conv1d gate reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects Top-K experts; experts read hidden states $\mathbf{H}$. \emph{(ii)}~\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA, Figure~\ref{fig:srmoa_arch}, architecture-agnostic validation): no external router, each expert has its own sigmoid gate on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$. \emph{(iii)}~\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}, diagnosis-actionability proof): each expert combines a shared NLinear raw-input branch with a gated backbone residual, which closes the DLinear gap.
492	
493	\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic (SR-MoA).} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, SR-MoA~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree} replaces the external Conv1d router with a per-expert sigmoid gate $\sigma_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})$, with no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$ ($15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT), confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. A third architecture-level control, \textbf{AdaMix-Raw} (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}), replaces AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router and recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells. All three router instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) confirm the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight converging controls.

504	C1 & RevIN ablation & Is RevIN the cause? & Entropy $0.000 \to 0.66$--$1.32$ (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}) \\
505	C2 & MOMENT vs Timer-XL & Same code, only norm differs & Opposite trajectories (Fig.~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}) \\
506	C3 & BatchNorm1d / GroupNorm & RevIN-specific or general? & All 3 normalizers collapse identically (App.~\ref{app:norm_generalization}) \\
507	C4 & Rescue sweep (5 families) & Optimization problem? & 0/11 configs recover; $2.7{\times}$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}) \\
508	C5 & AdaMix + raw router & Router architecture or input? & Entropy $\to 1.41$--$1.57$; MSE $-41$--$88\%$ (App.~\ref{app:adamix_details}) \\
509	C6 & SR-MoA raw vs hidden & Generalizes beyond RR-MoA? & Hidden: $+87$--$768\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}) \\
510	C7 & Vision ViT + InstanceNorm & Domain-specific? & Same collapse on CIFAR-10 (App.~\ref{app:vision_moe}) \\
511	C8 & $(\mu,\sigma)$ re-injection & Just append stats back? & $+42$--$239\%$ worse; 11/18 collapsed (App.~\ref{app:reinjection}) \\

515	
516	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why the simplicity of the fix is the point.} Identifying the correct cause is the hard part; that the fix follows trivially from the diagnosis is itself evidence the causal mechanism was correctly identified. The MoE community has long treated routing collapse as an \emph{optimization} problem (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss all attack the training dynamics), and these succeed when the router's input is informative but under-optimized. We show that normalization-induced collapse is a fundamentally different, \emph{information} problem: the routing signal is absent from the hidden states entirely, and none of the five rescue families (eleven configurations) we tested can compensate (720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}).}

> AGENT

Framing already crisp. Four explicit places where the categorical distinction is made:

1. **Contribution bullet (line 74)** — *"distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE-rescue literature"*
2. **Rescue paragraph (line 489)** — opens with *"To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned"* and closes with *"when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, none of the standard rescue mechanisms we tested can compensate"*
3. **Causal-controls table row C4 (line 507)** — column header literally reads *"Optimization problem?"* with answer *"0/11 configs recover"*
4. **Closing paragraph (line 516)** — *"The MoE community has long treated routing collapse as an optimization problem… We show that normalization-induced collapse is a fundamentally different, information problem"*

The opposition is explicitly **optimization vs information**, not just "rescue mechanisms fail." The sweep is positioned as a negative control falsifying the "it's just optimization" alternative — exactly the framing that makes using NLP-derived mechanisms as a control fair.

No edits needed. The reviewer pushback path you'd worry about ("you tested out-of-domain tools") is already pre-empted because the paper frames the test as "we're testing whether your alternative hypothesis (optimization pathology) explains the result — it doesn't." That's the correct use of those tools.

2605	
2606	\textbf{What this does and does not say about the paper's core claims.} This finding does \emph{not} undermine the central diagnosis of the paper: normalization-induced routing collapse on hidden-state routers (AdaMix) is a real, mechanistically-explained phenomenon that affects every TSFM with internal RevIN, and pre-normalization routing (RR-MoA) is the minimal fix. That diagnosis is independent of whether the MOMENT backbone is the most efficient architecture for forecasting on every dataset: it would remain true if the TSFM were replaced by any other backbone with internal instance normalization. What this finding \emph{does} say is that the dual-stream gap-closing story should be reframed: rather than ``the TSFM has complementary nonlinear features that dual-stream extracts,'' the more accurate reading is ``the TSFM contributes complementary signal on datasets with nonlinear dynamics (where it wins by $1$--$6\%$), and contributes essentially nothing on datasets where DLinear is already near-optimal (where pure raw-MLP MoE matches or beats it).''
2607	
2608	\textbf{Why we report this rather than hide it.} A pure raw-MLP MoE ablation was not in the original submission and was added in response to a reviewer who pointed out that, given Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}'s finding that the TSFM destroys nonlinear temporal structure, the obvious test of whether the TSFM is dead weight was missing. The reviewer's intuition was partially correct: the TSFM is dead weight on Weather, ETTm2, and Electricity, but not on the temperature-data datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1). We include the full result here because hiding it would invite the same attack at the next round of review, and because the dataset-conditional contribution of the TSFM is itself an interesting empirical pattern that deserves attention from the TSFM-design community. The honest takeaway: \emph{frozen TSFMs are useful where forecasting requires nonlinear temporal modeling beyond what a 5-MLP ensemble can express, and unnecessary where it does not}. The single most important consequence for our paper is that the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone: it explains the AdaMix-collapse phenomenon and predicts the cross-backbone behavior regardless.
2609

/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/main.tex:429:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). Two distinct mechanisms contribute. First, \emph{within MoE adapters}, unfreezing triggers gradient co-adaptation (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}): the dominant expert reshapes the shared backbone, collapsing routing, and freezing prevents this loop and preserves expert diversity. Second, \emph{across architectures}, the frozen five-expert mixture with learned per-sample routing provides an architectural advantage that a single unfrozen head cannot match even with full parameter access: per-sample expert selection captures input-regime structure that no single topology can represent. Within RR-MoA, frozen is best on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by up to $13\%$ on the other two. A second architecture introduced below, \textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA), in which each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input rather than a shared external router, independently replicates this pattern (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Even with careful hyperparameter tuning (learning rates $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, 100 epochs, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay, weight decay sweep, gradient accumulation up to effective batch 512, 90 configurations), full fine-tuning still loses by $51$--$71\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}).}

/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/main.tex:568:In the limit where the router's signal lives entirely in the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), the bound saturates and $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution. We therefore use the \emph{signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ as a tractable monotone proxy for the variance contribution of the stripped statistics. The bound is empirically tight: CCA gives $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by KSG~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}; a held-out classifier shows normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy with bound (ii) gap averaging $0.075$ nats (Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). /Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/main.tex:658:\paragraph{Implication.} Routing collapse on instance-normalized backbones generalizes a broader pattern: when a foundation model's input pipeline destroys signal that a downstream router needs, optimization-side rescues (load balancing, z-loss, ReLU routing) cannot recover what is structurally absent. The fix is to restore the missing input, not to retune the optimizer. 1643	\subsection{AdaMix Implementation Details}
1644	\label{app:adamix_details}
1645	
1646	Our AdaMix baseline follows \citet{wang2022adamix} with $K{=}5$ expert adapter heads identical to RR-MoA's canonical pool (mean, last, max, attention, conv1d). The router is a single linear layer $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^K$ operating on the mean-pooled hidden state, with softmax gating. We use a load-balancing auxiliary loss with coefficient $\lambda_\text{bal}{=}0.01$, matching AdaMix's original formulation. No stochastic routing, capacity factors, or noise injection are applied, since these standard MoE safeguards do not address the normalization-specific signal loss we identify: when RevIN strips the per-window statistics that would distinguish samples, the router receives near-identical inputs regardless of stabilization strategy. This is confirmed empirically: load-balancing loss does not prevent collapse under unfreezing (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}, entropy $= 0.000$ with $\lambda_\text{bal}{=}0.01$), while disabling RevIN recovers entropy to $0.66$--$1.32$ without any routing regularization.
1647	
1648	\textbf{Architecture-agnostic validation (AdaMix-Raw).} To confirm the diagnosis generalizes beyond RR-MoA, we replace AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input Conv1d router (identical architecture to RR-MoA's) while keeping AdaMix's expert heads and training loop unchanged. Table~\ref{tab:adamix_raw} shows results across 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds (36 runs).

2021	\section{Deployment-Regime Motivation}
2022	\label{app:deployment}
2023	
2024	The frozen-backbone paradigm is motivated by three deployment regimes where full fine-tuning is infeasible:
2025	
2026	\textbf{(i) Multi-tenant cloud serving.} A single TSFM sits in GPU VRAM and serves thousands of tenants via lightweight, hot-swappable per-tenant adapters in host RAM. Per-tenant DLinear requires collecting, storing, and periodically retraining on each tenant's historical data ($O(N)$ training pipelines for $N$ tenants), whereas the frozen backbone is loaded once and adapter weights (${\sim}50$--$500$K parameters, ${\sim}0.2$--$2$\,MB) are swapped from host RAM in microseconds. At $N{=}1{,}000$ tenants, the adapter approach eliminates $1{,}000$ independent training jobs and enables instant onboarding of new tenants via zero-shot transfer, capabilities absent from per-tenant supervised baselines.
2027	
2028	\textbf{(ii) On-device and edge deployment.} One backbone is shipped with the device image; per-site adapters are updated over low-bandwidth links. Collecting each site's training data centrally is often impossible for privacy or latency reasons.
2029	
2030	\textbf{(iii) Cross-task reuse.} The same frozen backbone drives forecasting, imputation, and classification via different expert pools. We demonstrate the first two tasks explicitly in the main text.
2031	
2032	\subsection{Inference Benchmark}
2033	\label{app:benchmark}

All three architectural fixes (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) add only single-digit milliseconds of adapter overhead on top of the backbone forward pass; the frozen-backbone fast-inference property is preserved by each.}

2055	The RR-MoA routing overhead ($+3.1$\,ms) is dominated by the sparse expert selection loop; the router itself (Conv1d + linear, ${\sim}1.1$K params) adds $<0.1$\,ms. SR-MoA dense and Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} both run \emph{faster} than RR-MoA Top-2 on GPU because their dense per-expert execution parallelizes over the $K{=}5$ expert dimension without per-sample sparse-routing kernel launches. Notably, Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} has \emph{fewer} adapter parameters than RR-MoA ($354$K vs $426$K) thanks to the shared NLinear raw branch.
2056	
2057	At deployment scale, adapter swapping between tenants requires loading $426$K parameters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB) from host RAM, orders of magnitude cheaper than reloading a $35$M parameter backbone. At $N{=}100$ tenants, adapter-swapping throughput is $141$ tenants/sec. The memory footprint of a shared-backbone deployment ($1\times$ TSFM at $140$\,MB plus $100\times$ RR-MoA adapters at $1.7$\,MB each $= 310$\,MB total) is $45\times$ smaller than naively replicating the full backbone per tenant ($100 \times 140$\,MB $= 14\,000$\,MB). \textbf{Honest caveat:} this $45\times$ figure is against the naive per-tenant-TSFM baseline, which no rational deployer would run; against per-tenant DLinear ($100 \times 49$K parameters $= 19.6$\,MB total) the shared-TSFM approach is roughly $15\times$ \emph{larger}, not smaller. The memory argument for TSFMs over DLinear is therefore not the core motivation; that role is played by cross-task reuse, zero-shot onboarding, and the elimination of $O(N)$ per-tenant training pipelines (see \S\ref{sec:intro} and Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}).
2058

SR-MoA dense and Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} both run \emph{faster} than RR-MoA Top-2 on GPU because their dense per-expert execution parallelizes over the $K{=}5$ expert dimension without per-sample sparse-routing kernel launches. Notably, Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} has \emph{fewer} adapter parameters than RR-MoA ($354$K vs $426$K) thanks to the shared NLinear raw branch.

2057	At deployment scale, adapter swapping between tenants requires loading $426$K parameters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB) from host RAM, orders of magnitude cheaper than reloading a $35$M parameter backbone. At $N{=}100$ tenants, adapter-swapping throughput is $141$ tenants/sec. The memory footprint of a shared-backbone deployment ($1\times$ TSFM at $140$\,MB plus $100\times$ RR-MoA adapters at $1.7$\,MB each $= 310$\,MB total) is $45\times$ smaller than naively replicating the full backbone per tenant ($100 \times 140$\,MB $= 14\,000$\,MB). \textbf{Honest caveat:} this $45\times$ figure is against the naive per-tenant-TSFM baseline, which no rational deployer would run; against per-tenant DLinear ($100 \times 49$K parameters $= 19.6$\,MB total) the shared-TSFM approach is roughly $15\times$ \emph{larger}, not smaller. The memory argument for TSFMs over DLinear is therefore not the core motivation; that role is played by cross-task reuse, zero-shot onboarding, and the elimination of $O(N)$ per-tenant training pipelines (see \S\ref{sec:intro} and Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}).

Figure 5: Left: Frozen Paradox, frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by 12–79%. Right: Observation 1
validated (ρ=−0.88, p<0.002). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases.


In the limit where the router’s signal lives entirely in the stripped statistics (E ⊥⊥ S | (M, Σ)), the
bound saturates and I(X; E) − I(S; E) = H(E): RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution. We
therefore use the signal ratio R(D) = [Var(M ) + Var(Σ)]/Var(S) as a tractable monotone proxy
for the variance contribution of the stripped statistics. The bound is empirically tight: CCA gives
ε ∈ [0.09, 1.26] nats, cross-validated within ±0.26 nats by KSG [25]; a held-out classifier shows
normalization retains only 16–41% of routing entropy with bound (ii) gap averaging 0.075 nats
(Appendix M). Training α ∈ [0, 1] as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to α < 0.5
on all six datasets (30/30 runs; Appendix L). R(D) predicts the raw-routing benefit at Spearman
ρ=−0.88 (p<0.002, n=9; Figure 5); H(E | S) alone does not (ρ=−0.12), since routing potential
in the stripped statistics matters, not the MI loss itself. Traffic (R=0.14, ∆=+2.9%) is correctly
predicted as a boundary case; Solar (R=0.06) is the one outlier (SSR ablation +43%; Appendix G).
Full proof in Appendix D.
Cross-backbone, task and horizon generalization. RR-MoA wins all 21 MOMENT-small/large
configurations (27–81%; Table O.1), 18/18 Moirai (3–31%), and 6/6 Moirai-MoE [12] datasets
(37–90%; Table O.2): adapter-level and backbone-internal routing operate on complementary axes.
The negative controls predicted by Observation 1 (Chronos and Timer-XL [10], neither using instance
normalization) show no collapse and no RR-MoA gain (4/18 within chance; Appendix O). Top-2
sparse routing retains most of the dense gain at a +10% latency cost (Appendix J); imputation (7/8;
Appendix K) and horizons H∈{96,192,336,720} (24/24; Table C.1) confirm robustness. Residual-
IA+ (Appendix Q.1) extends to all 6 datasets across 5 backbones and 4 horizons (Table Q.7).

2606	
2607	\textbf{Routing entropy diagnostics.} In all $30$ Raw-MLP MoE runs, routing entropy saturates near $\log K = 1.609$ (range $1.20$--$1.60$, mean $\approx 1.49$), indicating the router degenerates to near-uniform mixing. This means the Raw-MLP MoE is operating as a learned ensemble of $5$ size-diverse MLPs rather than as a per-sample mixture of specialists; the diversity comes from the heterogeneous expert capacities rather than from per-window routing decisions.
2608	
2609	\textbf{What this does and does not say about the paper's core claims.} This finding does \emph{not} undermine the central diagnosis of the paper: normalization-induced routing collapse on hidden-state routers (AdaMix) is a real, mechanistically-explained phenomenon that affects every TSFM with internal RevIN, and pre-normalization routing (RR-MoA) is the minimal fix. That diagnosis is independent of whether the MOMENT backbone is the most efficient architecture for forecasting on every dataset: it would remain true if the TSFM were replaced by any other backbone with internal instance normalization. What this finding \emph{does} say is that the dual-stream gap-closing story should be reframed: rather than ``the TSFM has complementary nonlinear features that dual-stream extracts,'' the more accurate reading is ``the TSFM contributes complementary signal on datasets with nonlinear dynamics (where it wins by $1$--$6\%$), and contributes essentially nothing on datasets where DLinear is already near-optimal (where pure raw-MLP MoE matches or beats it).''
2610	
2611	\textbf{Why we report this rather than hide it.} A pure raw-MLP MoE ablation was not in the original submission and was added in response to a reviewer who pointed out that, given Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}'s finding that the TSFM destroys nonlinear temporal structure, the obvious test of whether the TSFM is dead weight was missing. The reviewer's intuition was partially correct: the TSFM is dead weight on Weather, ETTm2, and Electricity, but not on the temperature-data datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1). We include the full result here because hiding it would invite the same attack at the next round of review, and because the dataset-conditional contribution of the TSFM is itself an interesting empirical pattern that deserves attention from the TSFM-design community. The honest takeaway: \emph{frozen TSFMs are useful where forecasting requires nonlinear temporal modeling beyond what a 5-MLP ensemble can express, and unnecessary where it does not}. The single most important consequence for our paper is that the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone: it explains the AdaMix-collapse phenomenon and predicts the cross-backbone behavior regardless.

"""he MoE community has long treated routing collapse as an optimization problem (load
balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss all attack the training dynamics), and these succeed when
the router’s input is informative but under-optimized. We show that normalization-induced collapse
is a fundamentally different, information problem"""


do you think this is a risky claim based on literature review

> AGENT

Yes, **medium risk** — survivable but worth softening.

### What's risky

1. **"Fundamentally different" is absolutist.** A reviewer only needs to cite ONE prior paper that frames routing as an information/representation problem to weaken this. Two existing precedents:

   - **Chi et al. (2022) "On the Representation Collapse of Sparse Mixture of Experts"** — argues that token representations themselves become too similar to route on. Their "representation collapse" is the closest semantic neighbor to your "normalization-induced collapse."
   - **Pham et al. (2024) "CompeteSMoE"** and recent self-routing work (AoE, ERMoE) frame routing quality as a representation problem, not purely an optimization one.

2. **The dichotomy "optimization vs information" is too clean.** Load balancing arguably addresses *both* — it forces diversity even when the router input is uninformative, by penalizing collapse directly. A reviewer can say "you're not testing a different category, you're testing whether load balancing is *strong enough*."

3. **The framing "MoE community has long treated routing collapse as an optimization problem"** is empirically slightly false. Some 2022-2024 papers (Chi et al. especially) DO frame it as a representation problem. Reviewers from that thread will push back.

### What's defensible

The empirical result itself is rock-solid: the rescue sweep IS a falsification test, and 0/11 configurations recovering MSE is a strong negative result. The interpretation just needs to soften the absolutist framing.

### Recommended rewording

Change:

> "We show that normalization-induced collapse is a fundamentally different, *information* problem"

to:

> "We show that normalization-induced collapse cannot be reached by these optimization-side mechanisms, because the failure is upstream: the router's *input* is structurally stripped of the discriminating signal by an architectural inductive bias (RevIN), not by training dynamics. This complements representation-collapse phenomena studied in NLP MoE \citep{chi2022representation_collapse}, where token representations become indistinguishable post-training; in our case, they are indistinguishable *before* training even starts, by design of the normalization layer."

That:
- Drops "fundamentally different" (the risky absolutist part)
- Acknowledges Chi et al. as the closest prior work
- Differentiates: their collapse is *post-training feature similarity*; yours is *pre-training architectural input stripping*
- Keeps the sharp empirical claim ("cannot be reached by these mechanisms") which the 720-run sweep supports

### Want the edit?

Yes/No — if yes, I'll also add `chi2022representation_collapse` to the bibliography. The paper currently doesn't cite it, which is itself a small risk (reviewer-as-author of that paper would notice).

Existing methods commonly achieve an expert-centered bal\u0002ancing strategy to solve it, prioritizing equal utilization of experts over semantic\nalignment between tokens and experts. However, this can lead to a pseudo-balance\nphenomenon: To ensure expert load balancing, the same input is randomly routed\nto different experts across training steps instead of the most matching one. It intro\u0002duces two critical issues: (1) Severe knowledge overlap among experts, resulting\nin redundant representations and inefficient parameter utilization. (2) Difficulty\nin forming and stabilizing expert specialization. These issues limit the scalability\nof models, especially large language models(LLM). To address these limitations,\nwe introduce Memory-Aware Routing (MAR), an approach that enhances exist\u0002ing load-balancing strategies. By equipping each expert with a memory buffer,\nour method explicitly models their long-term preferences, allowing historical ex\u0002perience to guide routing. This ensures that tokens are routed more consistently\nto compatible experts, mitigating the pseudo-balance problem while maintaining\nglobal load balance and fostering expert specialization. The remaining experts sit idle, consuming memory and adding model parameters that contribute nothing to the output. To address this issue, RevIN proposes a simple yet effective normalization method called reversible instance normalization (RevIN), a generally-applicable normalization-and-denormalization method with learnable affine transformation. The proposed method is symmetrically structured to remove and restore the statistical information of a time-series instance, leading to significant performance improvements in time-series forecasting, as shown in Figs below.\n\n![RevIN](figures/revin.png)\n\n### Quick Start\n\nkeras\n\n```python\nimport tensorflow as tf\nfrom tensorflow.keras import layers\nfrom revin.revin_keras import RevIN\n\ndata = tf.reshape(tf.range(0, 24), shape=(4, 3, 2))/24\n\nrevinlayer = RevIN()\ninputs = layers.Input(shape=(3, 2))\nx = revinlayer(inputs, mode='norm')\nx = layers.Conv1D(2, kernel_size=1, activation='relu')(x)\noutputs = revinlayer(x, mode='denorm')\n\nmodel = tf.keras.Model(inputs=[inputs], outputs=[outputs])\n```\n\npytorch\n\n```python\nimport torch\nimport torch.nn as nn\nfrom revin.revin_torch import RevIN\n\nx = torch.reshape(torch.range(0, 23), shape=(4, 3, 2))/24\n\nrevinlayer = RevIN(2)\n\nclass Net(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self):\n        super(Net, self).__init__()\n        self.revinlayer = RevIN(num_features=2)\n        self.conv1d = nn.Conv1d(in_channels=2, out_channels=2, kernel_size=1)\n\n    def forward(self, x):\n        x = self.revinlayer(x, mode='norm')\n        x = self.conv1d(x)\n        x = nn.ReLU(x)\n        x = self.revinlayer(x, mode='denorm')\n        return x\n```\n\n### Conclusion\n\nJust interested in the first implementation and welcome to test and ask questions.\n\n### Acknowledgments\n\n- [HyperTS](https://github.com/DataCanvasIO/HyperTS): A Full-Pipeline Automated Time Series (AutoTS) Analysis Toolkit.\n- [RevIN](https://github.com/ts-kim/RevIN): The official PyTorch implementation."

      "text": "Input Domain Aware MoE: Decoupling Routing Decisions from Task Optimization in Mixture of Experts\n\n# Input Domain Aware MoE: Decoupling Routing Decisions from Task Optimization in Mixture of Experts\n\nYongXiang Hua https://orcid.org/0009-0008-8849-4717 University of Science and Technology of ChinaState Key Laboratory of Cognitive IntelligenceHefeiChina yx15333063290@mail.ustc.edu.cn, Haoyu Cao https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3789-9705 University of Science and Technology of ChinaState Key Laboratory of Cognitive IntelligenceHefeiChina caohaoyu@mail.ustc.edu.cn, Zhou Tao https://orcid.org/0009-0005-4433-4373 University of Science and Technology of ChinaState Key Laboratory of Cognitive IntelligenceHefeiChina zhoutao24@mail.ustc.edu.cn, Bocheng Li https://orcid.org/0009-0005-2171-7902 University of Science and Technology of ChinaState Key Laboratory of Cognitive IntelligenceHefeiChina bcli@mail.ustc.edu.cn, Zihao Wu https://orcid.org/0009-0007-2199-8518 University of Science and Technology of ChinaState Key Laboratory of Cognitive IntelligenceHefeiChina zihaowu@mail.ustc.edu.cn, Chaohu Liu https://orcid.org/0009-0001-7588-4264 University of Science and Technology of ChinaState Key Laboratory of Cognitive IntelligenceHefeiChina liuchaohu@mail.ustc.edu.cn and Linli Xu https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0227-3793 University of Science and Technology of ChinaState Key Laboratory of Cognitive IntelligenceHefeiChina linlixu@ustc.edu.cn\n\n(2025)\n\n###### Abstract.\n\nSparse Mixture of Experts (sMoE) has become a pivotal approach for scaling large vision-language models, offering substantial capacity while maintaining computational efficiency through dynamic, sparse activation of experts. However, existing routing mechanisms, typically based on similarity scoring, struggle to effectively capture the underlying input structure. This limitation leads to a trade-off between expert specialization and balanced computation, hindering both scalability and performance. We propose Input Domain Aware MoE, a novel routing framework that leverages a probabilistic mixture model to better partition the input space. By modeling routing probabilities as a mixture of distributions, our method enables experts to develop clear specialization boundaries while achieving balanced utilization. Unlike conventional approaches, our routing mechanism is trained independently of task-specific objectives, allowing for stable optimization and decisive expert assignments. Empirical results on vision-language tasks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing sMoE approaches, achieving higher task performance and improved expert utilization balance.\n\nLarge Multimodal Model, Visual Question Answering, Mixture of Experts, Load Balancing\n\n††journalyear: 2025††copyright: acmlicensed††conference: Proceedings of the 33rd ACM International Conference on Multimedia; October 27–31, 2025; Dublin, Ireland††booktitle: Proceedings of the 33rd ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM ’25), Octo",

      "title": "[2512.23447] Coupling Experts and Routers in Mixture-of-Experts via an Auxiliary Loss",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23447",
      "publishedDate": "2025-12-29T07:17:41.000Z",
      "text": "[2512.23447] Coupling Experts and Routers in Mixture-of-Experts via an Auxiliary Loss\n\n# Computer Science > Computation and Language\n\narXiv:2512.23447 (cs)\n\n[Submitted on 29 Dec 2025 (v1), last revised 24 Feb 2026 (this version, v2)]\n\n# Title:Coupling Experts and Routers in Mixture-of-Experts via an Auxiliary Loss\n\nAuthors: Ang Lv, Jin Ma, Yiyuan Ma, Siyuan Qiao\n\n> Abstract:Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models lack explicit constraints to ensure the router's decisions align well with the experts' capabilities, which ultimately limits model performance. To address this, we propose expert-router coupling (ERC) loss, a lightweight auxiliary loss that tightly couples the router's decisions with expert capabilities. Our approach treats each expert's router embedding as a proxy token for the tokens assigned to that expert, and feeds perturbed router embeddings through the experts to obtain intermediate activations. The ERC loss enforces two constraints on these activations: (1) Each expert must exhibit higher activation for its own proxy token than for the proxy tokens of any other expert. (2) Each proxy token must elicit stronger activation from its corresponding expert than from any other expert. These constraints jointly ensure that each router embedding faithfully represents its corresponding expert's capability, while each expert specializes in processing the tokens actually routed to it. The ERC loss is computationally efficient, operating only on $n^2$ activations, where $n$ is the number of experts. This represents a fixed cost independent of batch size, unlike prior coupling methods that scale with the number of tokens (often millions per batch). Through pre-training MoE-LLMs ranging from 3B to 15B parameters and extensive analysis on trillions of tokens, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the ERC loss. Moreover, the ERC loss offers flexible control and quantitative tracking of expert specialization levels during training, providing valuable insights into MoEs.\n\narXiv-issued DOI via DataCite\n\n| Comments: |\n| --- |\n| Subjects: | Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG) |\n| Cite as: | arXiv:2512.23447 [cs.CL] |\n| (or arXiv:2512.23447v2 [cs.CL] for this version) |\n\n## Submission history\n\nFrom: Ang Lv [view email] [v1] Mon, 29 Dec 2025 13:03:18 UTC (3,561 KB) [v2] Tue, 24 Feb 2026 09:29:19 UTC (3,598 KB)\n\nFull-text links:\n\n## Access Paper:\n\n- View PDF\n- TeX Source\n\nCurrent browse context:\n\ncs.CL\n\n< prev| next >\n\nChange to browse by:\n\n### References & Citations\n\n- Google Scholar\n- Semantic Scholar\n\nexport BibTeX citation\n\n### Bookmark\n\nBibliographic Tools\n\n# Bibliographic and Citation Tools\n\nBibliographic Explorer Toggle\n\nBibliographic Explorer (What is the Explorer?)\n\nConnected Papers Toggle\n\nConnected Papers (What is Connected Papers?)\n\nLitmaps Toggle\n\nLitmaps (What is Litmaps?)\n\nscite.ai Toggle\n\nscite Smart Citations (What are Smart Citations?)\n\nCode, Data, Media\n\n# Code, Data and Media Associated with this Article\n\nalphaXiv Toggle",

      "text": "[2410.19123] Read-ME: Refactorizing LLMs as Router-Decoupled Mixture of Experts with System Co-Design\n\n# Computer Science > Computation and Language\n\narXiv:2410.19123 (cs)\n\n[Submitted on 24 Oct 2024]\n\n# Title:Read-ME: Refactorizing LLMs as Router-Decoupled Mixture of Experts with System Co-Design\n\nView PDF HTML (experimental)\n\n> Abstract:The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has led to the adoption of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures that dynamically leverage specialized subnetworks for improved efficiency and performance. Despite their benefits, MoE models face significant challenges during inference, including inefficient memory management and suboptimal batching, due to misaligned design choices between the model architecture and the system policies. Furthermore, the conventional approach of training MoEs from scratch is increasingly prohibitive in terms of cost. In this paper, we propose a novel framework Read-ME that transforms pre-trained dense LLMs into smaller MoE models (in contrast to \"upcycling\" generalist MoEs), avoiding the high costs of ground-up training. Our approach employs activation sparsity to extract experts. To compose experts, we examine the widely-adopted layer-wise router design and show its redundancy, and thus we introduce the pre-gating router decoupled from the MoE backbone that facilitates system-friendly pre-computing and lookahead scheduling, enhancing expert-aware batching and caching. Our codesign therefore addresses critical gaps on both the algorithmic and system fronts, establishing a scalable and efficient alternative for LLM inference in resource-constrained settings. Read-ME outperforms other popular open-source dense models of similar scales, achieving improvements of up to 10.1% on MMLU, and improving mean end-to-end latency up to 6.1%.       "text": "Decoupling of Experts: A Knowledge-Driven Architecture for\nEfficient LLMs\nNovember 18, 2025\nAbstract\nCurrent large language models (LLMs), particularly Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants, face challenges in achiev\u0002ing efficient, structured, and interpretable scaling. We introduce the Decoupling of Experts (DoE) architecture, a novel\nframework that addresses these limitations by grounding computation in a hierarchically organized and dynamically\nupdated knowledge space. Our methodology features a two-stage lifecycle: we first use Latent Dirichlet Allocation\n(LDA) to build a semantic topic foundation from the training corpus. This knowledge is then integrated into the main\nLLM, where it is dynamically refined. Critically, we discard traditional, static MoE experts. Instead, the expert entity\nis a dynamic Knowledge Block synthesized on-the-fly by reusing the Key and Value matrices from the attention\ncomputation. We replace the standard load balancer and softmax gating with an Attention Gating Control (AGC)\nthat employs a VAE-based router with a ReLU activation for expert composition. This entire process is optimized\nwith a composite loss function, balancing next-token prediction with a KL-divergence-based expert loss. Our analysis\nreveals that this architecture induces a remarkable heterogeneous specialization across layers, with some layers dif\u0002ferentiating into ”science” and ”humanities” domains, while others converge on general functions. This demonstrates\na learned, hierarchical division of labor, paving the way for a new, more efficient scaling dimension based on the\nnumber of structured experts.\n1 Introduction\nThe scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to unprecedented capabilities [3, 13]. The Mixture-of-Experts\n(MoE) paradigm [17, 15] has emerged as a key strategy for this, yet it suffers from its own pain points, including rout\u0002ing inefficiencies and the opaque nature of its randomly initialized experts. We argue that a more effective scaling path\nlies in partitioning the model’s knowledge into a structured, interpretable hierarchy, creating a new scaling dimension\nbased on the number and complexity of decoupled experts.\nTo achieve this, we introduce the Decoupling of Experts (DoE) architecture. Our methodology is founded on a\ntheory of emergent knowledge hierarchy built upon a matrix-based memory layer. We define a structure progressing\nfrom latent knowledge embeddings to Knowledge Blocks (collections of related knowledge), which emerge through\ntraining to form functional skills, or ”bricks.” An expert, in our framework, is a composition of these learned skills.\nThe key innovation is a two-stage training lifecycle that manages this knowledge. As illustrated in Figure 1, Stage 1\nuses Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) [1] to perform offline clustering, providing an initial semantic topic signal for\neach token. In Stage 2, the LLM is trained with a dual-input embedding: the standard token embedding plus this initial\nknowledge signal. "
